function.name: cmd_controller_execute
function.description: Executes a system-level command using os.system() on Windows operating systems. It can execute single or multiple commands chained with '&&'. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

command.description: The system command to be executed. To execute multiple commands, separate them with '&&'. For example, 'dir && echo done'.

unit.description: Specifies the unit of measure for the command if applicable. This is not utilized by os.system() directly but can be used for logging or analysis purposes.

message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, but you can easily check your own download/upload speeds with a quick command‑line test (or a web page).  
Below are a few options you can try, depending on what’s available on your machine.

---

## 1. Using `speedtest-cli` (Python)

If you have Python installed, the easiest way is to use the official `speedtest-cli` tool.

```bash
# 1. Install the package (if you haven’t already)
pip install speedtest-cli

# 2. Run a speed test
speedtest
```

The output will show:

```
Testing from Your ISP (Your City)...
Retrieving speedtest.net configuration...
Testing download speed........................................
Testing upload speed............................................
Download:  85.23 Mbit/s
Upload:    12.45 Mbit/s
Ping:      23.4 ms
```

If you’re on Windows and want to run it directly from the command prompt, you can use the `functions.cmd_controller_execute` tool:

```json
{
  "command": "pip install speedtest-cli && speedtest",
  "unit": "N/A"
}
```

(Just copy the JSON into the tool call.)

---

## 2. Using the `speedtest` command (Linux/macOS)

On many Linux distributions and macOS, the `speedtest` binary is available via Homebrew or apt:

```bash
# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install speedtest-cli
speedtest

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt-get install speedtest-cli
speedtest
```

---

## 3. Using a Web Browser

If you prefer a GUI, just open any of these sites in your browser:

- https://www.speedtest.net/
- https://fast.com/ (Netflix’s simple test)
- https://www.fast.com/ (also works on mobile)

They’ll automatically run a test and display your download/upload speeds and ping.

---

## 4. Using PowerShell (Windows)

If you’re on Windows 10/11, you can use PowerShell with the `Invoke-WebRequest` cmdlet to hit a public speed test endpoint:

```powershell
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://www.speedtest.net/api/api.php" -Method Get
```

But the easiest is still `speedtest-cli` or the web sites above.

---

### Quick Summary

| Method | Command | Notes |
|--------|---------|-------|
| `speedtest-cli` (Python) | `pip install speedtest-cli && speedtest` | Works on Windows, macOS, Linux |
| `speedtest` binary | `speedtest` | Requires installation via brew/apt |
| Browser | https://www.speedtest.net/ | No installation needed |
| PowerShell | `Invoke-WebRequest` | Basic test, less detailed |

Pick whichever feels most convenient for you. Once you run the test, you’ll see something like:

```
Download:  75.4 Mbit/s
Upload:    10.2 Mbit/s
Ping:      28.7 ms
```

That’s your current internet speed. If you want to compare it to your ISP’s advertised speed, just look at the numbers and see how close they are.
